Two Tables of the Law
too TAY-buhlz uhv thuh law
noun
From Exodus 31:18 and 34; the two tables of stone on which the LORD wrote the Ten Commandments.

📖 Biblical Definition

The two tables of the law are the two tablets of stone on which the LORD wrote the Ten Commandments with His own finger and gave to Moses on Mount Sinai. He gave unto Moses two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God; and the tables were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, graven upon the tables. When Moses, descending and seeing the golden calf, broke the first tables, the LORD commanded two new tables to be hewn, on which He wrote again the words that were in the first. The church has long understood the Ten Commandments as falling into two parts, fitly answering the two tables: the first table (the first four commandments) sets forth our duty toward God—to have no other gods, to make no graven image, not to take His name in vain, to keep the sabbath; the second table (the last six) sets forth our duty toward our neighbour—to honour father and mother, and not to kill, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet. This division is the very one the Lord gave when He summed the whole law in two commandments: to love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and thy neighbour as thyself; on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets. The dictionary honors the two tables of the law as the abiding summary of human duty—love to God and love to neighbour—written by the finger of God, summed by Christ, and the rule of life for the people of God in every age.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The two stone tablets on which God wrote the Ten Commandments; the first table our duty to God, the second our duty to neighbour, summed by Christ in love to both.

expand to see more

TWO TABLES OF THE LAW, the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments.

Written with the finger of God, given to Moses at Sinai (Exo 31:18).

The first table: our duty toward God (the first four commandments).

The second table: our duty toward neighbour (the last six).

Summed by Christ: love God, and love thy neighbour (Mat 22:40).

📖 Key Scripture

Exo 31:18 — "And he gave unto Moses, when he had made an end of communing with him upon mount Sinai, two tables of testimony, tables of stone, written with the finger of God."

Exo 34:1 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, Hew thee two tables of stone like unto the first: and I will write upon these tables the words that were in the first tables, which thou brakest."

Mat 22:37 — "Jesus said unto him, Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind."

Mat 22:40 — "On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The law’s two tables are sundered—piety without love of neighbour, or social ethics without God; Scripture binds both, summed in love to God and neighbour.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond the sundering of the tables. The corruption is the sundering of the two tables—keeping the one while neglecting the other. Some embrace the first table, a piety toward God, while despising the second, the love of neighbour; James and John warn that he who loves not his brother whom he hath seen cannot love God whom he hath not seen. Others seize the second table, a social ethic of duty to man, while casting off the first, the worship and fear of God—a benevolence without the God who commands it. Both tear apart what God joined.

The principle to recover is the unity and order of the two tables, summed by Christ. The LORD wrote both with His own finger (Exo 31:18; Exo 34:1): the first table our duty toward God, the second our duty toward neighbour. And the Lord Jesus bound them together when He summed the whole law: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart (Matt 22:37), the first and great commandment, and the second like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself; on these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets (Matt 22:40). The order matters: love to neighbour flows from love to God and is not its substitute. The two tables together are the abiding rule of human duty—not piety without mercy, nor mercy without piety, but love to God expressing itself in love to neighbour.
